rounds.prompt: What is stored in age after this line runs?

why: undefined is what a box holds when it gets no value, like let age; on its own. Here age is given 24.
'24' with quotes is a string (text). 24 without quotes is a number.
Nothing sets age to 0. The value on the right of = is what gets stored.

reveal.say: Before any line runs, the engine scans the code and makes a box called age. It isn't ready to use yet.
Line 1 runs: the engine works out the value 24 and stores it, so age holds 24. Now age can be used.

why: 2 was the first value, but line 2 replaces it with x * 3.
* means multiply, not join. x * 3 is 2 × 3 = 6, not "2" followed by "3".
x has a value by the time it is printed, so it isn't undefined.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes a box called x. It isn't ready yet.
Line 1: x is created with the value 2.
Line 2: the engine reads x (2), multiplies by 3, and writes 6 back into the same box.
Line 3: console.log reads x and prints 6.

why: 2 is the score after the first pass, but the body runs 3 times.
4 is the score after two passes. The loop runs for i = 0, 1 and 2: three passes.
8 would need 4 passes. When i reaches 3, i < 3 is false and the loop stops.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes a box for score. There is no i yet: i belongs to the loop.
Line 1: score is created and set to 0.
Line 2: the loop makes its own box i = 0, then checks i < 3. It's true, so the body runs.
Pass 1: the engine works out 0 + 2, so score becomes 2.
Back to line 2: i++ makes i = 1. The check is true again, so the body runs.
Pass 2: score becomes 4.
Line 2 again: i++ makes i = 2. Still true, so one more pass.
Pass 3: score becomes 6.
Line 2: i++ makes i = 3. Now the check is false, so the loop stops.
The loop is finished, so its box i is thrown away. Line 5 prints score: 6.

why: 5 is what goes in (n). The function returns n * 2, so 10 comes out.
double has a return, so result gets the returned value, not undefined.
n * 2 is the instruction, not the answer. The engine works it out (5 * 2) before returning.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine stores the whole function double, and makes a box for result that isn't ready yet.
Line 4 calls double(5). A new frame goes on top of the call stack, with its own box n = 5.
Inside the frame, line 2 works out n * 2. That's 5 * 2, so it returns 10.
The frame pops off the stack and its box n goes with it. Back on line 4, result = 10.
Line 5: console.log prints result: 10.

why: 3 never prints: the program stops on line 2, before console.log runs.
const means the box can't be given a new value, so pi never becomes 4.
pi has a value (3). The problem is changing it, not reading it.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes a box called pi. It isn't ready yet.
Line 1: pi is created as a const with the value 3.
Line 2 tries to give a const a new value. The engine stops with a TypeError, so line 3 never runs.

why: JavaScript doesn't fill an empty box with 0. You have to give it a value.
null only appears if someone stores it on purpose.
Reading a box that exists is fine. It just has no value yet.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes a box called score. It isn't ready yet.
Line 1: score is created but given no value, so it holds undefined.
Line 2 prints what the box holds: undefined.

why: Each lives++ changes the box. It doesn't just read it.
There are two lives++ lines, so 1 is added twice.
++ is an instruction, not text. It is never printed.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes a box called lives. It isn't ready yet.
Line 1: lives starts at 3.
Line 2: lives++ adds 1, so lives becomes 4.
Line 3 does it again: lives becomes 5.
Line 4 prints 5.

why: b got a copy of the number when line 2 ran. Changing a later doesn't touch b.
Nothing adds a and b together.
b was given a value on line 2, so it isn't undefined.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes boxes for a and b. Neither is ready yet.
Line 1: a gets 1.
Line 2 copies the value in a into b. Now b holds 1 in its own box.
Line 3 changes only a's box: a = 9.
Line 4 prints b, which still holds 1.

why: 16 < 20 is still true, so the body runs one more time.
n only ever doubles: 4, 8, 16, 32. It never equals 20.
Once n is 32, 32 < 20 is false and the loop stops.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes a box called n. It isn't ready yet.
Line 1: n starts at 4.
Line 2 checks n < 20. It's true, so the body runs.
n doubles: n becomes 8.
Check again: 8 < 20 is true.
n becomes 16.
Check again: 16 < 20 is still true, so one more pass.
n becomes 32.
Check again: now it's false, so the loop stops.
Line 5 prints 32.

why: i goes up by 2 each time (i += 2), so it doesn't take 6 steps to reach 6.
i = 4 still passes the check (4 < 6), so there is a third pass.
When i reaches 6, 6 < 6 is false, so there is no fourth pass.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes a box for count. There is no i yet: it belongs to the loop.
Line 1: count starts at 0.
Line 2: the loop makes i = 0 and checks i < 6. It's true.
Pass 1: count becomes 1.
Back to line 2: i += 2 makes i = 2. Still true.
Pass 2: count becomes 2.
i += 2 makes i = 4. Still true.
Pass 3: count becomes 3.
i += 2 makes i = 6. Now the check is false, so the loop stops.
The loop's i is thrown away. Line 5 prints count: 3.

why: The function works out 5 but never returns it, so the 5 is lost.
a and b are numbers, so + adds them. But that sum is never returned anyway.
A function with no return gives back undefined, not null.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine stores the whole function add.
Line 4 calls add(2, 3). A new frame goes on the stack, with a = 2 and b = 3.
Line 2 works out a + b, which is 5. But there is no return, so the 5 is thrown away.
The frame pops off the stack. With no return, add gives back undefined, and console.log prints it.

why: That would be (2 + 3) squared. Each call is squared on its own first: 4 + 9.
That's 2 + 3 + 5. Each number is multiplied by itself, not added.
That's 6 squared. The calls are squared separately, then added.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine stores square and makes a box for total that isn't ready yet.
Line 4 first calls square(2). A new frame goes on the stack with n = 2.
Line 2 returns n * n, which is 4.
That frame pops. Now square(3) is called, with a brand-new frame where n = 3.
Line 2 returns n * n again, which is 9 this time.
Back on line 4: 4 + 9 is worked out and stored, so total = 13.
Line 5 prints 13.

why: change() runs before the print, and it changes the same x.
x is created on line 1, so it is never undefined.
x = 3 replaces the value. It doesn't add to it.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes a box for x (not ready yet) and stores the function change.
Line 1: x gets 10.
Line 3 calls change(). A new frame goes on the stack. It has no x of its own.
Inside change, x = 3 looks for x, finds the global one, and changes it. Now x holds 3.
The frame pops. Line 4 prints the global x: 3.

why: length counts every character from 1, so L-a-g-o-s is 5. (Indexes start at 0; length doesn't.)
The quotes aren't part of the text. Only L-a-g-o-s counts.
.length gives a number: how many characters there are.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes a box called word. It isn't ready yet.
Line 1: word gets the text "Lagos".
Line 2 counts the characters, L, a, g, o, s, and prints 5.

why: They look alike, but one is a number and one is a string. === needs both value and type to match.
=== answers a yes/no question, so it prints true or false.
Comparing a number with a string is allowed. It just isn't equal.

reveal.say: Before running, the engine makes boxes for a and b. Neither is ready yet.
Line 1: a gets the number 5.
Line 2: b gets the text "5". The quotes make it a string.
Line 3: === compares the value and the type. A number and a string are never ===, so it prints false.
